SSH and Remote Administration

1. SSH and Remote Administration

Remote access is both a tool and a dependency. HarborWorks cannot safely harden SSH by removing its only working login method. The requirement is stronger: trusted operators must retain a verified path, unauthorized users must be rejected, and recovery must remain possible when the network path fails.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — Chapter 12 — SSH and Remote Administration

2. Preserve an authenticated administration path

Verify the server host key and keep an independent recovery path before changing authentication policy. An SSH policy edit locks out the only working administrator session.

SOURCE: Preserve an authenticated administration path

3. Chapter 12 — SSH and Remote Administration

Remote access is both a tool and a dependency. HarborWorks cannot safely harden SSH by removing its only working login method. The requirement is stronger: trusted operators must retain a verified path, unauthorized users must be rejected, and recovery must remain possible when the network path fails.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — Chapter 12 — SSH and Remote Administration

4. 12.1 SSH Architecture

SSH establishes an encrypted connection, authenticates the server, authenticates the user, and carries channels such as an interactive terminal or file transfer. Server authentication and user authentication answer different questions. A user key proves something about the connecting user; a host key identifies the server being contacted.

Encryption alone does not protect you from connecting to an impostor whose key you accepted without checking. Establish the server’s host-key fingerprint through a trusted console or other independent channel. Record why a changed fingerprint is legitimate before replacing the old trust entry. (R29)

Linux example — 12.1

Inspect SSH's effective client choices without connecting.

What to check: This expands configuration for the lab alias; it does not validate the server's host identity.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.1 SSH Architecture

6. 12.2 OpenSSH

OpenSSH provides the commonly used ssh client and sshd server, together with key and transfer utilities. Installing the client does not necessarily install or enable the server. Package names differ: Debian/Ubuntu use openssh-client and openssh-server; RHEL-family systems commonly use openssh-clients and openssh-server.

Use the distribution’s supported package and cryptographic policy. Copying a years-old cipher list from a blog may weaken a modern default or conflict with compliance settings. Inspect the installed version and manual before using newer options. (R29, R30)

Linux example — 12.2

Check the installed OpenSSH client version.

What to check: Client and server packages may be installed independently.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.2 OpenSSH

8. 12.3 SSH Clients and Servers

The client initiates the connection. The server listens and evaluates authentication and session policy. ssh operator@web1 means “connect as operator,” not “log in as whoever owns the client workstation.” Client and server configuration files also differ: ssh_config configures clients, while sshd_config configures the server.

On the RHEL baseline, the service is normally sshd.service. Ubuntu commonly uses ssh.service, and socket activation may make ssh.socket responsible for the listener. Inspect systemctl status ssh.service ssh.socket rather than assuming a service restart always reconfigures the listening socket.

Linux example — 12.3

Inspect the server configuration on the lab VM.

What to check: Syntax success does not prove the daemon is listening or reachable.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.3 SSH Clients and Servers

10. 12.4 Password Authentication

Password authentication sends proof through the encrypted SSH channel; it does not send the password as an unencrypted network login. Its risks include guessing, reuse, phishing, and stolen credentials. Rate controls and monitoring help, but they do not turn a weak shared password into accountable access.

Password authentication is distinct from keyboard-interactive authentication, which may use PAM and multifactor prompts. Disabling one directive does not necessarily disable every password-like path. Conversely, disabling keyboard-interactive blindly can break an approved multifactor design. Test the effective policy for the actual account and source.

Linux example — 12.4

Request password authentication explicitly for an approved lab server.

What to check: Enter the password only at the prompt; verify the host key through a trusted channel first.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.4 Password Authentication

12. 12.5 Public-Key Authentication

A key pair has a private key kept by the user and a public key the server can authorize. The server verifies a cryptographic proof; the private key should not be copied to the server. A passphrase protects a stored private-key file, but it is not the account’s login password.

Keys need an owner, purpose, approval, rotation/revocation path, and protection. An untracked key in a shared account is not automatically safer operationally than a managed credential. Separate personal interactive keys from limited-purpose automation keys and remove authorization when its purpose ends.

Linux example — 12.5

Use an existing dedicated lab key.

What to check: The public key must already be authorized; the private key stays on the client.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.5 Public-Key Authentication

14. 12.6 Generating SSH Keys

For an ordinary non-FIPS lab where policy permits Ed25519, create a separate teaching key on admin1:

Choose a passphrase interactively. Do not overwrite an existing key. Environments with approved cryptographic requirements may require a different supported algorithm, such as policy-approved RSA. The filename without .pub is private; the .pub file is the public half. Inspect the public fingerprint with ssh-keygen -lf ~/.ssh/harbor_lab.pub.

Linux example — 12.6

Generate a fresh key without overwriting an existing one.

What to check: Use a passphrase when prompted; protect the private file and share only the .pub file.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.6 Generating SSH Keys

17. 12.7 authorized_keys

The target account’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys normally contains authorized public keys, one per line. Restrictive ownership and permissions prevent another user from altering access. A typical personal setup uses mode 700 for .ssh and 600 for authorized_keys, owned by the target account; parent directories must also satisfy the server’s checks.

Key lines can restrict behavior, including forwarding or permitted commands. Such restrictions are valuable for backups and automation, but a forced-command wrapper must safely validate inputs. Do not grant a general interactive root key merely because a scheduled task needs to read a particular directory. SELinux labeling can also affect access on enforcing systems.

Linux example — 12.7

Inspect authorized-key path permissions for your own account.

What to check: Missing files mean key authorization is not yet set up; do not blindly overwrite them.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.7 authorized_keys

19. 12.8 SSH Configuration

A client alias in ~/.ssh/config reduces repeated typing:

Use only the verified address and account. ssh -G harbor-web1 displays the expanded client settings. On the server, included files, ordering, and Match blocks affect the effective configuration. Many OpenSSH settings use the first obtained value; a later drop-in is not automatically an override. Inspect effective settings rather than judging the last line you edited. (R29)

Linux example — 12.8

Print effective SSH client configuration.

What to check: Inspect hostname, user, identityfile, and proxyjump for the intended lab target.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.8 SSH Configuration

22. 12.9 Secure SSH Configuration

The safe order is establish console access, create a named administrator, install and verify a key, verify that administrator’s approved sudo rights, validate the server configuration, apply the change, and test a new session before closing the old one. Prefer accountable named accounts to routine direct root login.

sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -t validates server syntax. sudo /usr/sbin/sshd -T displays effective settings; use -C with representative connection parameters when Match rules matter. A policy might disable direct root login and password authentication after key access is proven. That policy is a reviewed outcome, not a universally safe block to paste. Keep the configured port unchanged during the first hardening exercise; changing a port is not a replacement for authentication.

Linux example — 12.9

Validate the server before applying any hardening.

What to check: Match blocks require appropriate -C connection values; test a second session before closing the first.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.9 Secure SSH Configuration

24. 12.10 SCP

scp provides a familiar source-to-destination file-copy interface over SSH. Modern OpenSSH versions normally use SFTP internally; legacy protocol behavior can differ in quoting and filename expansion. Inspect the installed manual rather than assuming shell wildcards behave identically across releases.

For a single explicitly named file, scp report.txt harbor-web1:report.txt copies into the target account’s home directory. Verify the host identity first, then compare the transferred file’s size or hash as appropriate. A successful copy is not a deployment: ownership, destination validation, activation, and rollback still need handling.

Linux example — 12.10

Copy a lab report to an approved account.

What to check: Review the destination before copying; the transfer overwrites a same-named remote file.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.10 SCP

26. 12.11 SFTP

SFTP is a file-transfer protocol carried through SSH, not FTP with an added password. An interactive sftp harbor-web1 session supports commands such as ls, put, and get. Local and remote current directories are distinct, so inspect them before moving data.

Restricted SFTP-only access can be useful for transfer accounts. Chroot configurations impose strict directory-ownership requirements and are easy to misconfigure. Build them from the installed OpenSSH documentation, not by giving the restricted user ownership of the entire jail root. Verify both permitted transfers and denied shell access.

Linux example — 12.11

Open an interactive SFTP session.

What to check: At the sftp prompt, use pwd, ls, and quit; review destinations before put or get.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.11 SFTP

28. 12.12 rsync over SSH

rsync -a -e ssh source/ harbor-web1:destination/ uses SSH as transport and synchronizes the source directory’s contents. The trailing slash matters: source/ selects contents, while source can introduce the directory itself. Start with --dry-run --itemize-changes to see the proposed operation.

Archive mode preserves several common attributes, but does not automatically include every ACL, extended attribute, or hard-link requirement. Remote privileges and filesystem support also matter. Avoid --delete until the exact source and destination are proven; a mounted backup target disappearing can turn a familiar path into the wrong destination. (R49)

Linux example — 12.12

Preview an SSH-based synchronization.

What to check: The trailing source slash copies contents; dry-run previews without transferring.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.12 rsync over SSH

30. 12.13 SSH Tunneling

A local forward carries connections through SSH to a destination reached from the server side. For an authorized lab-only service on web1 loopback:

Connect locally to http://127.0.0.1:18080/. The first address restricts the client-side listener to loopback; the second loopback address is interpreted on the remote side. Keep the process in the foreground for this lab and stop it with Ctrl-C. A tunnel can cross intended boundaries, so it requires authorization rather than being a workaround for denied access.

Linux example — 12.13

Forward a local-only port to the lab server.

What to check: While open, localhost:8080 reaches the server's loopback port 80; Ctrl-C closes the tunnel.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.13 SSH Tunneling

33. 12.14 SSH Agent

An SSH agent holds usable signing identities so you do not repeatedly unlock the same key. ssh-add -l lists loaded identities; ssh-add -t 1h ~/.ssh/harbor_lab limits how long a loaded identity remains available in a running agent.

Agent forwarding exposes access to the agent through a remote socket. A compromised remote host may misuse that access to authenticate elsewhere while it is available, even without extracting the private-key file. Prefer a jump-host connection that keeps signing on the client, and enable forwarding only for a reviewed need. (R29)

Linux example — 12.14

Inspect keys already loaded in the SSH agent.

What to check: An unavailable agent or empty key list is diagnostic information, not a reason to disclose private keys.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.14 SSH Agent

35. 12.15 Bastion Hosts

A bastion is a deliberately controlled entry point to a restricted environment. It concentrates access policy and monitoring but also becomes an important security and availability dependency. Keep its software minimal and its administrative ownership clear.

ssh -J approved-bastion internal-host uses a jump host without requiring private keys to be copied onto it. The final host still needs its own verified identity. Do not weaken host-key checking simply because traffic passed through a trusted intermediate system. Document a recovery path when the bastion is unavailable.

Linux example — 12.15

Connect through an approved bastion.

What to check: Both aliases must be configured and their host keys verified; do not enable agent forwarding by habit.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.15 Bastion Hosts

37. 12.16 Troubleshooting SSH

Classify the failure before editing settings. A timeout suggests an unanswered path; refusal commonly means no accepting listener or an explicit rejection; a host-key warning is an identity problem; “Permission denied” occurs after reaching authentication. These categories lead to different tests.

Use ssh -vv harbor-web1 for bounded client evidence and the corresponding service journal on the server. Review offered key, selected account, effective configuration, account state, home ownership, key-file permissions, and SELinux context. Debug output can expose names, paths, and public-key information, so sanitize it before sharing.

Linux example — 12.16

Capture an interactive diagnostic connection.

What to check: Identify whether failure occurs in transport, host-key checking, or authentication; redact infrastructure details before sharing output.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — 12.16 Troubleshooting SSH

39. Requirement and simplest approach

HarborWorks wants hb-operator to use a dedicated key and approved sudo permissions. The account must already exist, and a verified initial login or console must be available. Merely setting PasswordAuthentication no first would remove the bootstrap path before proving its replacement.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — Requirement and simplest approach

40. Selected procedure

On admin1, generate the teaching key as shown earlier and verify the server’s fingerprint independently. Install only the public key with an approved method, such as ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/harbor_lab.pub hb-operator@192.168.56.10 where the initial authentication method is permitted. Confirm file ownership on web1 rather than assuming the transfer utility solved every policy issue.

Open a new terminal and connect with the explicit key:

Inside that session, run id and sudo -l. The latter should show the permissions intentionally assigned in Chapter 4, not an expectation that every lab account automatically has full administration rights. Test an approved harmless elevated command if one is granted.

On the server console, back up the exact SSH configuration files being changed. Make the reviewed authentication-policy change, then validate:

For account/source-specific rules, inspect with a connection specification such as:

Replace every connection value with the intended test. Apply through the installed service arrangement. A configuration reload may suffice for authentication changes; a socket-activated listener change requires the distribution’s socket-specific procedure. Do not restart a guessed unit.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — Selected procedure

45. Verification and recovery

Keep the original session open until a fresh connection succeeds. Test rejection of the authentication path you intentionally removed, without repeatedly locking out an account. If the test fails, restore the backed-up configuration through the existing session or console, validate, apply, and retest. Record the successful and rejected paths.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — Verification and recovery

46. Practice and implementation lab

Create a host alias for web1, inspect it with ssh -G, and transfer a harmless file through SFTP. Compare its hash on both ends. Explain where the private key, authorized public key, and trusted host key are stored and why these are three separate responsibilities.

Check your understanding. Is known_hosts the list of users permitted to log in? No; it records server identities. Does an existing SSH session prove new authentication works? No. Does moving SSH to another port replace a strong authentication policy? No.

Chapter takeaway. Secure remote administration preserves a verified authorized path while deliberately closing unauthorized ones.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch014.xhtml — Practice and implementation lab

47. Reject a changed recorded host identity

Compare invented identity records. Real SSH uses its host-key verification tools, not this simplified text record. The solution checks the stated outcome explicitly. These fixture results do not establish that a real privileged service is configured correctly.

SOURCE: Reject a changed recorded host identity
